newsitem.title: USA: Unemployment steady at 5.3 percent in December.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment steady at 5.3 percent in December.

text.p: The unemployment rate held steady at 5.3 percent in December, the government said on Friday, as the economy created new jobs at a stronger-than-expected pace in most major industries.
The surprisingly strong job data fuelled fears of inflation and higher interest rates.

The Labour Department said the jobless rate was unchanged last month after November's rate was revised downward to 5.3 percent from an earlier reported 5.4 percent. The department said 262,000 jobs were created outside the farm sector in December after a revised jump of 127,000 in November.
Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had pegged the December unemployment rate at 5.3 percent and predicted that roughly 192,000 jobs would be created.

"There was a real sharp rise in earnings, the market won't like it and it's going to make the Fed nervous," said Ward McCarthy, managing director at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc. "It's just going to resurrect concerns that labour market conditions are too tight."

U.S. Treasury bonds fell sharply on the news, which reignited fears that the Federal Reserve would boost interest rates to keep inflation in check. The benchmark 30-year bond slid 1-13/32 of a point, or $14.0625 per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, jumped to 6.87 percent from 6.75 percent late Thursday.
The department said the report reflects its routine end-of-year revisions for seasonal factors.
The December report follows a string of recent data that have pointed so far to an economy that was strengthening at the end of 1996.
For all of 1996, a total of 2.6 million new jobs were generated, compared with an increase of 2.2 million in the year before.

Average hourly earnings by workers, closely watched because of the role wage inflation plays in pushing up consumer prices, rose six cents an hour last month after rising nine cents an hour in November.
The report showed that the length of the average workweek rose to 34.8 hours from 34.5 hours in November.

Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs in December after adding 9,000 in November. Factory overtime hours rose to 4.7 hours from 4.5 hours in November, while the factory work week was up at 42.0 hours from 41.7 hours.
Construction added 23,000 jobs after adding 14,000 in November. Service-producing industries added 222,000 jobs after gaining 96,000 in November.
